facts.text: On this date in 1961, East Germany began erecting the Berlin Wall overnight — by morning, families who had gone to sleep in one country woke up permanently separated from relatives 200 meters away.
Today in 1521, Tenochtitlan fell to Hernán Cortés, ending the Aztec Empire. The city had a population larger than any in Europe at the time.
The Philippines is the only country in the world where divorce remains fully illegal for non-Muslim citizens — even legal separation doesn't dissolve the marriage.
More people live within a 4,000 km radius centered on Bangladesh than outside it — roughly half of all humanity packed into one circle on the map.
Tokyo's greater metropolitan area holds 37 million people, making it larger than the entire populations of Australia and New Zealand combined.
On August 13, 1979, Business Week ran its infamous 'The Death of Equities' cover. The S&P 500 proceeded to rise roughly 2,000% over the next two decades.
On August 13, 1997, the Dow Jones crossed 8,000 for the first time — a level that would briefly feel like a ceiling, then like a floor, then like ancient history.
The New York Stock Exchange was founded under a buttonwood tree in 1792 with just 24 brokers. The agreement they signed was 43 words long.
Saudi Aramco's 2019 IPO raised $25.6 billion — the largest in history — yet the company sold less than 2% of itself. It valued the whole enterprise at $1.7 trillion.
The word 'salary' comes from the Latin 'salarium,' a Roman soldier's allowance to buy salt. The commodity was once scarce enough to be legal tender across the ancient world.
On this date in 1961, East Germany sealed the Berlin Wall border — but biology sealed something stranger: your body replaces its entire skeleton roughly every 10 years, one silent cell at a time.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its matter would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.
On August 13, 2003, Europe recorded its hottest temperature in centuries during a heatwave that killed 70,000 people — heat the human body resists partly by sweating up to 1.5 liters per hour.
The universe is not silent — it hums at a frequency about 57 octaves below middle C, a gravitational wave background discovered to be washing through everything, including you, right now.

Your eyes move roughly 100,000 times a day, and the brain quietly erases the blur from each movement so your visual world appears perfectly stable — a seamless illusion constructed entirely after the fact.
On this day in 1521, Tenochtitlán fell to Cortés — ending a city larger than any in Europe at the time. London would not surpass its population for another century.
On this day in 1961, East Germany began building the Berlin Wall. It stood for 28 years — exactly as long as it had been down by 2017.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. Lectures began around 1096; Tenochtitlán was founded in 1325.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. She died in 30 BC; Khufu's pyramid rose around 2560 BC.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — before the American Civil War, before the telephone, and 14 years before India's first war of independence.
Mamihlapinatapai (Yaghan): the wordless look shared by two people who both want something but neither will initiate. One of the world's most succinct words — and one of the hardest to translate.
Sonder (coined 2012, Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows): the realization that every passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Too useful to remain unofficial.
On this day in 1521, the Aztec capital Tenochtitlán fell — and with it, Nahuatl's reign as a lingua franca. The language survives, giving English 'chocolate,' 'avocado,' and 'tomato.'
Hiraeth (Welsh): a longing for a home you cannot return to, or that never existed. It folds homesickness, grief, and nostalgia into a single syllable-cluster English simply cannot match.
On this day in 1889, the word 'cordite' entered official British military records, naming the new smokeless propellant. It comes from 'cord' — the explosive was extruded in long, thin strings.
On this date in 2010, Laszlo Hanyecz made the first real-world Bitcoin purchase — two pizzas for 10,000 BTC. At Bitcoin's 2021 peak, those pizzas cost roughly $690 million.
On Aug 13, 2021, OpenSea's Discord was hacked and fake minting links drained user wallets — exposing that NFT security risk lived entirely off-chain, not in the smart contracts.

Ethereum's base fee is permanently burned, not paid to validators. Since EIP-1559 launched in 2021, over 4 million ETH have been destroyed, making the network deflationary during high-traffic periods.

Bitcoin's script language was deliberately crippled by Satoshi — opcodes for multiplication and string operations were disabled in 2010 after a value overflow exploit nearly let someone print infinite BTC.

The largest single Bitcoin transaction ever recorded moved 500,000 BTC in one block in 2011 — coins belonging to Mt. Gox consolidating its cold wallets, briefly terrifying the market into thinking an exchange had collapsed.

On this date in 2006, Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues published the paper that revived deep learning by showing deep belief networks could be pre-trained greedily, layer by layer — ending a two-decade winter for neural networks.

On this date in 2012, the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge results were being tabulated. AlexNet would soon post a top-5 error of 15.3%, beating the runner-up by 10.8 percentage points — a margin that stunned the computer vision field.

GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed around 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity — roughly the annual consumption of 4,500 average US homes, spent on a single model before a single user query was served.

Transformers, now the dominant architecture in AI, were introduced in 2017 specifically to replace recurrence in machine translation. The authors named the paper 'Attention Is All You Need' as a deliberate provocation, not a description of a general theory.

AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — essentially the entire known protein universe — in roughly 18 months. The same work would have taken the global structural biology community thousands of years by experiment.
